newsitem.title: UK: Chile forex move fuels rate cut hopes - Dresdner KB.
newsitem.headline: Chile forex move fuels rate cut hopes - Dresdner KB.

text.p: Moves to revalue the Chilean peso this week set the scene for an interest rate cut by the end of March, but the move is not positive for the equity market overall, Dresdner Kleinwort Benson said on Friday.
On Monday, Chile's central bank announced it was changing the composition of the currency basket against which the peso exchange rate is set, in an effort to drive down inflation.

It also widened the peso's floatation band against the dollar since its recent appreciation against the peso (up 2.8 percent in three months) was pushing up import prices and braking the fall in inflation.

"The latest changes to the exchange rate system should be seen as a way of laying the foundations for a future cut in interest rates, without jeopardising this year's inflation target," Dresdner Kleinwort Benson's Latin American strategist Joe MacHatton said.
Chile has a 5.5-percent inflation target for 1997.
"By tightening the exchange rate system, the way has been paved for an interest rate cut...We expect a 50 basis point reduction in short rates by the end of March."
But he said the move would have a neutral to slightly negative impact on growth of GDP and earnings, and may have a secondary negative effect of discouraging investors.

The measures, which effectively revalued the peso by four percent against the dollar, boosted the price of Chilean stocks for foreign buyers who reacted by dumping local shares and Chilean ADRs. The market rebounded on Thursday, but traders say the surge is unlikely to persist.

The change in basket weights means Chile now has a greater exposure to changes in the U.S. dollar. It shifted to an 80 percent weighting from 45 percent previously, while the mark and yen weightings were reduced.
"With the switch in basket weights, any appreciation of the dollar in the foreign exchange market will have a much larger impact on the peso, dragging it up behind the dollar," MacHatton said.

He said the stronger peso was moderately negative for manufacturers and mining companies, but lower interest rates would spur domestic economic activity, which would be positive for banks and retailers.
But the move may hurt stock multiples in general and MacHatton said he maintained an underweight recommendation.
"Local pension funds and foreigners alike were looking forward to lower interest rates, but not a strengthening currency," he said.
"On balance, this is not good for the market." --Caroline Brothers, London Newsroom +44 171 542 2734
